findings.element: .tl-device and .tl-paperEdge — shell.css lines 279-289 (`border: 1px solid var(--ink-16)` / `var(--ink-10)`, both with `background: var(--paper)`), plus the inline patch `style: "border-color:var(--fore-16)"` on .tl-paperEdge in render-b.js states.desk (line 1544)
findings.problem: These are the only two objects in the lab still written against literal ink and paper rather than the fore/back ladder, and b.css opens by naming that as structural rule 2 ('NOTHING IS WRITTEN AGAINST INK OR PAPER'). The alpha border composites over the element's OWN hardcoded white background, not over the ground, so the ladder step is thrown away on the ink room. Pixel-sampled at 1440x960: .tl-device's edge is rgb(217,217,217) on both grounds — against the paper page (246) that is 1.31:1, the intended whisper; against the ink page (17) it is 13.38:1. .tl-paperEdge on desk is worse: the inline --fore-16 patch resolves to rgba(255,255,255,0.16) over #ffffff, i.e. rgb(255,255,255) — 18.88:1, byte-identical to --fore, the ink the 148px count is set in. So on the ink ground the loudest line in the room is the frame around the artifact: four times the contrast of the indigo rail (3.00:1) and eight times the foot's own hairline (--fore-16 = #414141, 1.59:1). It disfigures phone, day, ended, loading and loading-slow (.tl-device) and desk (.tl-paperEdge) — six of the fourteen graded states, on one of the two graded rooms. Neither gate can see it: audit.mjs grades text contrast only, and interaction-check asserts 'the ink ground paints ink' but nothing about the frame. The inline patch is the tell — the team already decided this edge must flip with the ground, and the fix was inert (in fact inverted) because the white background under it was never touched. Both rendered values, 1.00 and 0.86 effective alpha, are off the declared ladder entirely, in a file whose ladder comment says the whole point is 'there is no way for one of them to be forgotten, which is exactly how the first attempt at this left two controls painting white on white'.
findings.fix: In shell.css: change `.tl-device` to `border: 1px solid var(--fore-16); background: var(--back);` and `.tl-paperEdge` to `border: 1px solid var(--fore-10); background: var(--back);` — four token swaps, no new declarations. Leave the inline `border-color:var(--fore-16)` on .tl-paperEdge in states.desk (it is now correct, because the background beneath it is the ground). Rebuild with build.mjs. Verified by injecting exactly this at runtime and re-sampling the border pixel: ink phone 217 -> 55 (13.38:1 -> 1.59:1), ink desk 231/255 -> 41 (-> 1.30:1), and paper phone, paper desk and print all come back byte-identical to today (217, 231, 231). Print forces the paper ground, so --fore/--back resolve to ink/white there and the keepsake is unchanged. Add one assertion to interaction-check.mjs: for each room, sample the composited border pixel of .tl-device (or .tl-paperEdge) against the page pixel 4px outside it and require the ratio below 2:1 on both grounds — a frame that is louder than the accent is a frame that is wrong.

biggestWin: The two rooms are one design rather than two skins, and the proof is mechanical: nine fore/back tokens, a per-ground alpha on the one accent that could not survive both grounds, and a forced-colours map moved to the foot of b.css so it actually wins. Underneath that, five declared and gated ladders — ink, tracking, leading, space, size — mean 'slightly greyer' is not a thing anyone can reach for, and the 92 lines of comment explaining why each number is that number make this the rarest thing in a design lab: a file that can be inherited. The gesture itself holds up to driving — setAway is the single writer, every fact derives from the one date, the tick stays on the true pixel while the words are pushed clear, place() is a fixed point, and undo carries a closure and a scroll position per entry. Tab order at 1440 is three bar controls, seven Edit controls in list order, the disclosure, done — every stop on screen, every one named with its date and its distance.
